Marcar o ponto 3/10 na primeira reta numérica
Dividir a segunda reta numérica (John) em 3 partes iguais

Selecionar a alternativa correta e clicar em Done

erros.devolutiva: Explicar que alterar o denominador exige uma fração equivalente (ex: 1/3 = 3.3/10)

dicas.texto: Você está indo bem! Quando comparamos frações com denominadores diferentes, o que acontece se imaginarmos as duas retas uma embaixo da outra, começando no zero?
Tente marcar o ponto 3/10 na primeira reta e o ponto 1/3 na segunda. Depois, observe qual ponto está mais longe do zero.
Quase lá! Para comparar, tente encontrar um denominador comum ou apenas observe visualmente qual marcação fica mais à direita na reta numérica.
Pense assim: 1/3 é o mesmo que aproximadamente 0,33 e 3/10 é 0,30. Qual desses valores é maior na reta numérica?
Como podemos saber qual fração representa uma distância maior a partir do zero?
Compare a posição dos dois pontos marcados em relação ao '1' na reta numérica.
Observe: 1/3 é maior que 3/9, e 3/10 é menor que 3/9. O que isso diz sobre quem nadou mais?
Veja a posição final: o ponto de 1/3 está mais próximo do 1 do que o ponto de 3/10?

interfaceCtat.descricao: Interface FIXA do tutor (a mesma tela para todos os problemas): enunciado; DUAS retas numéricas de 0 a 1, uma para cada quantidade (rotuladas "Mile Bathany swam" e "Mile John swam"); para cada reta há um campo onde o aluno digita em quantas partes iguais dividi-la (com confirmação) e, depois, marca o ponto da fração correspondente; abaixo, um seletor em que o aluno escolhe UMA destas alternativas: "Coach should choose Bethany."; "Coach should choose John."; "Both are equally matched!"; botão Hint; botão Done. Os passos do aluno são ações NESSES componentes (dividir cada reta, marcar cada ponto, escolher a alternativa, concluir).

Mark Bethany's position at 3/10 on her number line.
Divide John's mile number line into 3 equal parts, then confirm.
Mark John's position at 1/3 on his number line.
Compare the two marked positions and identify the fraction to use for the coach's choice.
Select the coach's choice and click Done to finish.

dicas.texto: What does the denominator tell you about the number line?
Look at the bottom number in Bethany's fraction and use it as the number of equal parts.
Bethany's fraction is 3/..., so focus on the denominator rather than the numerator.
Enter the denominator of 3/... in the parts field and confirm the division.
A fraction on a number line tells you how many equal intervals to move from zero.
Start at zero, count the equal intervals, and stop after the number shown by the numerator.
Use three intervals from zero on the line divided into ten parts.
Click the third interval after zero, keeping the denominator as ten.
What does the denominator represent when a whole mile is divided?
Read the bottom number of John's fraction and use it to set the number of equal parts.
John's fraction is 1/3, so the relevant denominator is 3.
Enter 3 in John's parts field and confirm the division.
Use the numerator to decide how many intervals to move from zero.
Begin at zero and count one equal interval on John's three-part line.
The first interval after zero represents one third of the mile.
Click the first interval after zero and keep the denominator as three.
Compare the locations of the two marks on the same 0-to-1 scale.
Use the positions of ... and 1/3 rather than comparing only their numerators or denominators.
Look at which marked location the exercise identifies as the comparison target for the final choice.
Select the fraction shown as the required comparison result after inspecting both marks.
Use the two completed number lines as evidence for the coach's decision.
Compare the marked fractions and choose the swimmer indicated by the exercise's required result.
The relevant choice is the option naming Bethany, not the option naming John or a tie.
Select the Bethany option, then press Done to submit the completed comparison.

exercicio.statement:
Bethany and John's coach needs to pick a fast swimmer for a certain competition. The coach told each of them to swim a mile.  After some time has passed, the coach decided to check on their progress. Use the number line to help the coach see who has swum more.
Bethany swam 3/10 of a mile.
John swam 1/3 of a mile.
Who should the coach pick for the competition?

steps.instruction: Divide Bethany's mile number line into 10 equal parts, then confirm.
Mark Bethany's position at 3/10 on her number line.
Divide John's mile number line into 3 equal parts, then confirm.
Mark John's position at 1/3 on his number line.
Compare the two marked positions and identify the fraction to use for the coach's choice.
Select the coach's choice and click Done to finish.
